image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - Two-panel **line chart** (time-series line charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Faceting / small multiples**: two side-by-side panels comparing:
     - **Ten most vaccinated states**
     - **Ten least vaccinated states**
   - Each panel contains **two colored lines** for age groups.
   - A **shaded vertical band** marks a recent period labeled “REPORTING DELAYS POSSIBLE.”

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Date | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| New daily hospital admissions per 100,000 people | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Age group (Adults, Under 18) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of line; end labels |
| State group / vaccination category (Ten most vaccinated states, Ten least vaccinated states) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into left and right panels; panel titles |
| Reporting-delay period | Temporal interval | Shaded vertical band/background region with text label |

Difference of Data for Covid Hospitalizations
From the evidence provided in the article, it can be seen that while the 10 most and least vaccinated states start off May with a lowering rate of hospitalizations for adults and minors; there's a greater increase of those who need hospitalization in least vaccinated states. Although both sides have an increase of hospitalizations recently, it can be seen that the states with the least amount of vaccinations are having more cases of Covid-19. I wonder if the areas of the states which do/do not have the most vaccinations has anything to do with the rising or decreasing cases of the virus needing hospitalization. I'm also curious about if the hospitalizations recorded are more confirmed or suspected Covid-19 cases since it's stated that there's both on the graph. Relating to my community, this graph represents a neighboring state of mine which can be an accurate representation of how my state may be doing. It's among one of the 10 most vaccinated states in the country, and our vaccination rates are very similar. 
In this graph, there's a decline of virus cases for adults steadily until about August. In both cases of the least/most vaccinated states, there's a rise in cases but the less vaccinated states have more of an increase of hospitalizations for Covid-19. On the other hand, hospital cases for those 18 or under are decently consistent for both sides, but the less vaccinated states still have a raise in hospitalizations.

This could prove true that increased vaccination could decrease the amount of hospitalizations. As schools start up again, most students like me could benefit from getting vaccinated, as their likelihood of getting hospitalized is lower than adults.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

COVID hospitalization rates are much higher in adults in the ten least vaccinated states to the ten most vaccinated states. In both graphs, the COVID rates were going down before the Delta variant was introduced and both increased from that. 

2. What do you wonder?

The scale of this graph is not super clear and there will always be anti-vaxxers and even statistics don't convince people so what exactly is the purpose of this graph? Is it for the most vaccinated states bragging rights (Massachusetts being one of them) or is it to shame the least vaccinated states because I'm just not quite sure? 

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

COVID has had a huge impact on me and the community. Selfishly, I dance, and dancing in a mask is not easy. I'm not actually complaining though because millions of people have died of COVID. I know so many people who have gotten COVID (My mom included!)

4. What's going on in this graph? 

Vaccine or the hospital?

comments.raw_comment: In these graphs, I immediately notice that the ten most vaccinated states had far fewer hospital admissions due to Covid, over the past five months, compared to the ten least vaccinated states. Towards the end of the week, adults in the least vaccinated states' covid hospitalizations skyrocketed compared to the under eighteen children. A question I have about these graphs would be why adults in the most vaccinated states actually started with more covid hospitalizations than the least vaccinated states. It is not by much, but it is clear that the adults in the most vaccinated states actually had more covid patients hospitalized. These graphs relate to me, and everyone in the country, for clear reasons. Since the vaccine for COVID-19 has come out, it has been a mission for our country to get as many people as possible vaccinated so we can shorten these long and hard times. Personally, my family and most of my friends are vaccinated so we haven't had any personal issues with covid. This also relates to my school community because we were heavily affected by the pandemic, making school go online, cancelling social events, and creating new rules for everyone. A title for this graph could be, "Vaccinations affect on Hospitals: Positive or Negative?" Although it might be simple, it summarizes what these graphs are trying to explain in one sentence.

Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the number of hospital admissions per 100,000 people for the ten most and least vaccinated states.  The time series graphs are for May 1 - September 6, 2021.  The first cases of the Delta variant of Covid were identified in Texas on May 20.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “How does this relate to you and your community?”  

Plus, please share with us a headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, October 1 with moderation on Wednesday, October 6.  The topic:  Sunisa Lee’s Olympic gymnastic routine.  Keep noticing and wondering!

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, you can see that there is a tremendous difference in hospital admissions between the ten most and least vaccinated states. Something that I notice is that the ten most vaccinated states mostly consist of the northeastern states. The south appears to populate the most unvaccinated amount of people. It also appears that the vaccines seem to be working because of this drastic difference in hospitalization numbers. There has been an increase in hospitalizations for adults in both graphs mostly likely because of the new delta variant that has taken the world by storm. Another thing that I can infer is that the people who are 18 and younger are continuing to respond a lot better to the virus than adults. Something that I wonder is truly when this virus is going to get under control. There have been so many waves that the U.S. has gone through with the number of cases but it is so hard to see when this virus will be over. I also wonder why the southern region does not have nearly as many people vaccinated as the northeast. I think that this graph is trying to show that the vaccine truly makes a difference in numbers and decreases the amount of hospitalization. This graph relates to my community because I live in one of the ten most vaccinated states. With that said, people in my area are still getting the virus but compared to other states the numbers are a lot lower. A catchy headline that I have come up with is "Hospitalization Numbers Regarding Vaccine Numbers".

comments.raw_comment:
In the ten least vaccinated states, the number of daily hospital admissions has skyrocketed over the course of the past few months. Though the number had been slowly decreasing as we entered the summer months, more and more cases began to emerge. In the ten most vaccinated states, the number did drop significantly during the summer months. But compared to the ten least vaccinated states, cases did not significantly increase as summer began to fade. In both graphs however, the number of cases for people under 18 has remained mostly static. 

What I wonder is why more cases have not appeared in the least vaccinated states for people under 18. I would imagine that they would have more exposure to the virus. 

This relates to me in my community because I live in a state with a high vaccination rate. Despite that, we still have to abide by COVID-19 protocols and guidelines to keep everyone else safe. I wonder what it is like to go to school in a state with low vaccination rates, do they have more quarantining? Or does it stay the same?

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the number of hospital admissions per 100,000 people for the ten most and least vaccinated states.  The time series graphs are for May 1 - September 6, 2021.  The first cases of the Delta variant of Covid were identified in Texas on May 20.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “How does this relate to you and your community?”  

Plus, please share with us a headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, October 1 with moderation on Wednesday, October 6.  The topic:  Sunisa Lee’s Olympic gymnastic routine.  Keep noticing and wondering!
